## The idea

Three notes can survive enough change to organise a long melody. Repeat them
higher and the relationship is clear. Stretch their durations and the identity
weakens without disappearing. Keep only the first two and the fragment still
points back to its source.

A *motive* is a short musical idea that remains recognisable under
transformation. A *sequence* repeats it at another pitch level. *Development*
turns repetition into an argument by transposing, inverting, augmenting, or
fragmenting the source. Literal repetition establishes the object; controlled
change keeps it active.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 108
use_synth :pluck

cell = [60, 63, 62]
rhythm = [0.5, 0.5, 1]

define :play_phrase do |notes, durations|
  notes.zip(durations).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
end

define :transpose_notes do |notes, amount|
  notes.map { |pitch| pitch + amount }
end

define :invert_notes do |notes, axis|
  notes.map { |pitch| axis - (pitch - axis) }
end

bars = [
  [cell, rhythm],
  [transpose_notes(cell, 2), rhythm],
  [transpose_notes(cell, 5), rhythm],
  [invert_notes(cell, cell[0]), rhythm],
  [cell, rhythm.map { |duration| duration * 2 }],
  [cell.first(2) * 2, [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]],
  [transpose_notes(invert_notes(cell, cell[0]), 7), rhythm],
  [[60, 63, 62, 60], [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]]
]

2.times do
  bars.each { |notes, durations| play_phrase notes, durations }
end
```

The opening three-note cell returns at several levels, upside down, at twice its
duration, and as a fragment. Repeating the eight-bar plan produces a sixteen-bar
melody from one source object and a small transformation vocabulary.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the sequence offsets `2` and `5` with `1` and `2`. The sequence grows
   more tightly and may sound less like separate statements.
2. Move the inversion axis from the first note to 63. The same operation now
   reflects around another pitch and changes the register of the result.
3. Repeat the opening cell four times without transformation. Compare the point
   at which confirmation turns into stasis with the developed version.

## Why it works

Transposition adds one constant to every pitch, preserving interval sizes.
Inversion reflects signed distances around an axis: an upward minor third becomes
a downward minor third. Augmentation scales durations. Fragmentation selects a
subsequence. Each function preserves some invariants and discards others.

The bars array stores score decisions while `play_phrase` handles interpretation.
No transformed phrase needs copied note literals. If the source cell changes,
every derived occurrence updates. This is the musical value of avoiding duplicated
data as well as the engineering value.

A sequence becomes audible through repetition at successive pitch levels. Two
statements often establish the rule; later repetitions confirm it. The source
warning that four can bore is a compositional judgement to audition. The code
makes the count editable, so the claim can be tested rather than inherited.

Placement changes what a transformation does to form. A transposed cell placed
immediately after the source sounds like continuation. The same cell after eight
bars can sound like recollection. Register, cadence, and accompaniment alter the
connection further. The transformation functions capture pitch and duration
relationships; the `bars` plan supplies rhetorical position. Neither layer
replaces the other.

The closing four-note bar adds C after the original cell. That small extension
shows another development method: preserve the source and append a consequence.
Try prepending a note instead. The cell may stop sounding like the beginning of
the idea even though all its values remain present. Recognition depends on
boundary and emphasis as well as membership.

## Take it further

Write a sixteen-bar plan from one four-note motive. It must contain one literal
return, a three-step sequence, one inversion, one augmented statement, and one
two-note fragment. No bar may contain hand-copied transformed pitches. Print a
label before every bar so the generated structure can be compared with what you
hear.
